source.version: Journal version of record: Proceedings of the Design Society, Volume 6: DESIGN 2026, pp. 507-516, https://doi.org/10.1017/pds.2026.10409 (header of p. 507)
source.title_on_document: Evaluating TRIZ with and without LLM support: an experimental study on engineering problem-solving

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. All design-quality statistics are in the main text (Section 4.2 and Table 2, p. 512). Data and materials are available from the corresponding author on request (Data availability, p. 515).

paper_design_summary: Engineering students (114 analyzed) each solved one of three engineering concept problems (polymer gear testing rig GT, bicycle motor mounting bracket MB, wind turbine power maximization WT) and were randomly assigned to use the TRIZ contradiction matrix with an LLM assistant (TRIZ-C+LLM, Microsoft Copilot with GPT-5 recommended, plus a prompt pack) or the TRIZ contradiction matrix alone (TRIZ-C, triz40.com site, no LLM). PhD-holding experts rated each student's final developed solution on feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, and elaboration (1-7 scale), averaged into a design-quality score; a post-task survey measured self-reported workload, usefulness, and satisfaction.

studies.label: TRIZ-C+LLM vs TRIZ-C experiment on three engineering problems (GT, MB, WT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Method: TRIZ contradiction matrix with LLM support (TRIZ-C+LLM) versus TRIZ contradiction matrix only (TRIZ-C). The problem (GT, MB, WT) was not randomized: each problem was solved by a separate student group (course or program).
assignment.quote: Each student solved one problem only and was randomly assigned the method to use, either TRIZ-C+LLM or TRIZ-C.

arms.name: TRIZ-C+LLM
arms.description: TRIZ contradiction matrix supported by an LLM-based AI assistant; students received a prompt pack (problem framing, contradiction parameters, inventive principles, solution generation, diversity check) and were recommended Microsoft Copilot with Smart GPT-5 but free to choose another assistant. Analyzed per problem: GT 10, MB 10, WT 43 (Table 2).

arms.name: TRIZ-C
arms.description: TRIZ contradiction matrix only, with access to https://www.triz40.com/ and instructions not to use any LLM-based AI assistant. Analyzed per problem: GT 11, MB 10, WT 30 (Table 2).

participants.exclusions: One GT student did not understand the engineering problem and was excluded from the study (Table 1 note, p. 510); the GT curriculum count is ME (22) against N1 = 21. The paper does not say whether this student was excluded before or after assignment. One MB TRIZ-C+LLM student did not answer the survey, so survey analyses use 113 (62 vs 51); design quality uses 114. The paper gives no count at assignment.
participants.who: Engineering students: GT mainly fourth-year mechanical engineering (21); MB Erasmus exchange master students, mostly mechanical engineering (20); WT fourth- and fifth-year industrial engineering students specialized in AI (73).
participants.country: not_stated (author affiliations: Slovenia, Sweden, Morocco, Canada; Figure 2 names Location 2 for GT and MB and Location 3 for WT without naming countries)
participants.quote: N1: number of students performing the assignment, N2: number of students answering the questionnaire
participants.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Table 1 and note; p. 512 (PDF p. 6), Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Copilot with the LLM option Smart GPT-5 (recommended); students free to choose other LLM-based AI assistants but had to report which one
ai_tool.how_used: Students prompted the chatbot using a prompt pack with instructions and examples for problem framing, identifying TRIZ contradiction parameters, suggesting inventive principles, generating solutions, and a diversity check; then developed and documented their top-ranked idea (p. 511, Section 3.3, Figure 3).

task.description: Engineering concept problems solved individually with the TRIZ contradiction matrix: GT, a concept for alternating loading of polymer gears in a test rig; MB, a bracket mounting an electrical drive onto a bicycle frame; WT, a concept to maximize wind turbine power. Students found ideas from inventive principles and developed and documented their top-ranked idea. In WT a contradiction and its principles were imposed; in GT and MB students chose contradictions.
task.duration: Test planned to take about 45 minutes (students could use more or less time), preceded by a 30 min TRIZ presentation, 15 min of prompt engineering, and a practice problem (p. 511, Section 3.3). Reported completion time: TRIZ-C+LLM M = 40.3 min, TRIZ-C M = 46.2 min (p. 513).

outcomes.name: Design quality (expert-rated, mean of feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, elaboration)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts holding PhDs in mechanical engineering rated each final solution on four criteria on a 1-7 scale: C1 feasibility, C2 requirements, C3 innovativeness, C4 elaboration; design quality is the average of the four. GT and MB: two domain experts rated independently and their scores were averaged per criterion; WT: one independent expert rated all solutions. Only the composite is reported, not the separate criteria. Blinding to condition is not stated. The construct is a composite design-quality score in which innovativeness is one of four criteria, not a pure creativity rating.

contrasts.reported: Total: TRIZ-C 4.8 (SD 0.90, N 51) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 5.6 (SD 1.13, N 63). Two-way ANOVA (Problem x Method), Method main effect F(1, 108) = 3.21, p = .076, "which is not significant"; interaction F(2, 108) = 7.58, p = .001; Levene's test F(5, 108) = 2.88, p = .018.
WT: TRIZ-C 5.0 (SD 0.78, N 30) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 6.2 (SD 0.62, N 43); simple effect F(1, 108) = 34.67, p < .001.
GT: TRIZ-C 4.9 (SD 0.91, N 11) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 4.6 (SD 1.17, N 10); simple effect F(1, 108) = .51, p = .479.
MB: TRIZ-C 4.2 (SD 0.98, N 10) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 4.2 (SD 0.93, N 10); simple effect F(1, 108) = .06, p = .809.

data_and_code.data_url: available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (p. 515, Data availability)

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned to TRIZ with an LLM assistant or TRIZ alone (p. 510, Section 3.2.1); 114 students were analyzed across both arms (Table 2, p. 512); the outcome is expert-rated design quality of each student's solution, including an innovativeness criterion, on concept-generation problems. Caveats: the randomization procedure is not described and the WT arms are unbalanced (30 vs 43); the problem factor is not randomized; the outcome is a composite design-quality score rather than a creativity rating alone; within each problem the per-problem samples are small (GT 21, MB 20) and only WT (73) exceeds 50 on its own.

one_line_finding: Expert-rated design quality was 5.6 with an LLM vs 4.8 without (F(1,108) = 3.21, p = .076), with a problem-by-method interaction (p = .001): LLM support raised quality on the general WT problem (6.2 vs 5.0, p < .001) but not on the specialized GT (4.6 vs 4.9) or MB (4.2 vs 4.2) problems (p. 512, Table 2).
open_questions: Construct coding: design quality averages feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, and elaboration; coded overall_creativity here, but it could be coded other because innovativeness is only one of four criteria and the separate criteria are not reported.
Design class: coded lab_rct (a common protocol run in sessions at each site after a TRIZ presentation); GT and MB were part of a course, which could argue for field_rct.
Randomization: the paper states random assignment but gives no procedure; WT arms are 30 vs 43, which is uneven for simple 1:1 assignment.

Whether the per-problem groups should be separate samples or studies: each problem was solved by a different student group (Locations 2 and 3), and the paper analyzes them jointly in one two-way ANOVA.
Effects are confounded with problem and student group in the paper's own discussion: WT students specialized in AI and were more experienced in prompting (pp. 510, 514).
notes: Self-reported outcomes are excluded from the outcome list because they are not scored on the output: student satisfaction with their final concept (Table 2, in parentheses), workload items (difficulty defining contradictions t(111) = -4.123, d = -0.779; overall problem difficulty t(111) = -3.784, d = -0.715), self-rated innovation gain (p = .321), quality of generated ideas (p = .099), feasibility perception, enjoyment, perceived usefulness, and mental effort (p. 513, Figure 4). A pilot (Group 1, Location 1) tested the protocol and reports no outcome data. The students in the LLM arm could use assistants other than Copilot/GPT-5; the paper does not report which were used. Table 2 reports means to one decimal and SDs to two decimals.
